sample_data.reset_instructions: Run `npm run seed`. It loads case PUB-01 of the published P09 dataset from data/seed-case.json and is idempotent, so running it any number of times restores exactly the initial state: 27 owners, 42 vehicles, 165 service items, 99 service records, working date 2026-08-30. `npm run check:db` reports what is currently loaded.

problem_solving_method: The due-date rules are the whole problem, so they live in a pure module (lib/domain) with no database or React imports, and are covered by unit tests that run without a server. Everything else is a thin shell around that engine. Due dates and statuses are derived on every read rather than stored, which makes staleness structurally impossible after a service is recorded or the working date moves. Distance-based items are projected from each vehicle's own measured daily running, taken from its odometer history, so two vehicles on the same interval get different dates. The dataset states that 'today' is a field of the case and never the clock, so the application stores a working date that the user can change, and every estimate recalculates from it.

R1.evidence: 42 vehicles across 27 owners, each with 3-5 service items spanning all three rule types, odometer readings and past service records. Routes /vehicles and /vehicles/[id]; seeded by lib/seed/seed.ts from data/seed-case.json; counts verifiable at /api/health.

R2.evidence: lib/domain/due.ts computes a next due date per rule: fixed_date reads the expiry, period_months adds months to the last service with end-of-month clamping, distance_km projects from that vehicle's measured km/day. Every item is marked overdue / due soon / fine, and carries a plain-language basis string shown in the UI ('Runs 72.6 km/day - 1,240 km to go'). Visible on /vehicles/[id].

R3.evidence: Route / is the daily call list: one row per owner (not per vehicle, so a person with three vehicles is one call), with phone number, each vehicle, each due item and its reason. Ordered by a stated rule in lib/domain/priority.ts - clamped days-overdue of the worst item plus capped value of due work - printed on the page under 'How this list is ordered' and shown per row as its own arithmetic. Search with suggestions plus status filters.

R4.evidence: Route /owners/[id] shows every item with its next due date and cost; /vehicles/[id] records a completed service, which resets that item and appends to the service history. Single-item reset is enforced by a MongoDB arrayFilters update and proved against the live database by `npm run verify:reset` for all three rule types, plus an end-to-end test asserting every sibling item is unchanged.

eight_week_forecast.evidence: Route /forecast: eight weekly bars with item counts and value, busiest week emphasised, already-overdue work held in a separate backlog band.

odometer_entry_updates_estimates.evidence: 'Add odometer reading' on /vehicles/[id] recalculates the vehicle's daily running, which moves every distance-based due date on that vehicle.

copy_ready_reminder.evidence: features/owner/reminder.ts builds a plain-text reminder per owner naming each item and cost; shown with a Copy button on /owners/[id], and offered as a prefilled Gmail draft.

additional_features: Route /map: a home-service map. Every customer on the call list is plotted on a real map of Dhaka and grouped by neighbourhood so a round can be planned by geography. Selecting a customer zooms to them and draws the route from the workshop with distance and drive time. Leaflet with OpenStreetMap tiles; react-leaflet was avoided because its licence is outside the permitted families.
Route /dashboard: fleet health, work by rule, eight-week workload and outstanding value by item, with filters that redraw every chart and a table view of the same numbers.
Route /called: the day's contact record, with undo.
Email reminder: opens a prefilled Gmail draft (recipient, subject, body) and logs the owner as contacted. It never sends automatically.
Search with suggestions on the call list; search, status filters and sorting on the fleet.
Record a service directly from the call list.
Print stylesheet and CSV export of the day's list.
Dark and light themes, each with its own status palette, applied before first paint. Light is the default.

team_members.major_contribution: Sole developer. Built the entire project: the due-date engine, the data layer and seed, the call list, service recording, the dashboard, service map, contact log and email reminders, the test suite and the documentation.

major_design_decisions: The due-date engine is a pure module with no database or React dependency, so the rules can be unit tested without a server and the same code produces every figure on screen.
Due dates and statuses are computed on every read rather than stored. At 42 vehicles the pass is sub-millisecond, and nothing can go stale after a service is recorded.
The call list is keyed by owner rather than by vehicle: the workshop rings a person, so an owner with three vehicles is one call. This turned 41 vehicle rows into 27 calls.
Money is integer paisa throughout, formatted only at the edge, so no total drifts through floating point.

Dates are YYYY-MM-DD strings with their own arithmetic. new Date('2026-08-30') parses as UTC and shifts a day in local time, and setMonth overflows 31 Jan + 1 month into March - 113 records in the source data fall on the 29th-31st.
'Today' is a stored working date the user can change, because the dataset states that today is a property of the case and never the clock.
No authentication: no required feature involves user accounts, and a login would only stand between a judge and the application.

Email opens a prefilled draft rather than sending server-side. The event supplied no mail credential, the demo addresses are on the reserved example.com domain, and a workshop should see what is going to its customer before it goes.
known_limitations: Email is composed, not sent. The button opens a prefilled Gmail draft and the operator presses Send; there is no server-side mail delivery.

Owner email addresses are generated demo data on example.com, the domain IANA reserves for documentation. They accept no mail. Names, phone numbers and plates come from the organisers' published sample data and are synthetic.
Item costs are the expected price recorded against each item, not live quotes. The reminder message states this to the customer.
A distance-based item cannot be estimated for a vehicle with fewer than two odometer readings, or one that has not moved. Those are reported as 'no estimate' rather than given a fabricated date.
The service schedule per vehicle is seeded and cannot yet be edited in the interface; intervals come from the dataset.
The inline forms have no exit animation - they appear with a transition and close instantly.

The road route on the service map comes from a public OSRM demo endpoint. When it does not answer, the app falls back to its own straight-line distance and labels it as an estimate rather than presenting it as a measurement.

ai_tools_used.used_for: Implementation throughout: the due-date engine, the data layer and seed, the interface, the test suite and the documentation. Also used to analyse the published dataset before any code was written, which is where the month-end clamping requirement and the 'today is a case field, not the clock' constraint were identified.
ai_tools_used.how_output_was_verified: 86 unit tests over the pure engine, 51 end-to-end tests covering one block per required feature, and `npm run verify:reset`, which checks the single-item reset constraint against the live database for all three rule types. The engine's output was cross-checked against an independent model of the published dataset written separately: both report the same overdue and due-soon counts and the same total outstanding value. Interface work was reviewed against screenshots of the running application, which is how several defects were caught that no test covered - a chart rendering its numbers with no bars, a map legend showing three labels for two colours, and mobile layout overflow.
